questions.title: Docker Compose for Multi-Container Apps
questions.question: How does Docker Compose work and how do you set up a complete Java backend stack with it?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Docker Compose: orchestrate multiple containers with a single YAML file and docker compose up
- Services: each container is a service — app, db, redis, kafka
- depends_on: start order dependency (not health readiness — use healthcheck + condition)
- Networks: compose creates a default network; services reach each other by service name
- Volumes: define named volumes for persistent data
- Environment files: .env file for config values, secrets
- Profiles: selectively start services (--profile dev vs --profile prod)
- Docker Compose Watch (v2.22+): hot-reload for development

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Docker Compose lets you define an entire multi-container application in a single YAML file. Running docker compose up starts all defined services in the right order, creates networks so they can communicate by service name, and manages volumes for persistent data. It's the standard tool for local development and testing of multi-service applications.

The key services for a typical Java backend stack are the application itself, a PostgreSQL database, Redis for caching, and optionally Kafka for messaging. Each gets its own service definition with its image, environment variables, ports, and volume mounts. Services on the same Compose network can reach each other by their service name — the Spring Boot app connects to postgres:5432 and redis:6379 without any IP configuration.

The most important caveat with depends_on is that it only controls start order, not readiness. PostgreSQL may be accepting connections before it's finished initializing, and your Spring Boot app might connect too early and fail. The fix is to use depends_on with a health check condition, which waits until the dependency reports healthy before starting dependent services.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Complete Java Backend Compose File

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml
name: my-java-app

services:
  # ===== Spring Boot Application =====
  app:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: dev
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/appdb
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME: appuser
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
      SPRING_DATA_REDIS_HOST: redis
      SPRING_KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS: kafka:9092
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy  # wait for health check
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - app-network
    restart: unless-stopped

  # ===== PostgreSQL =====
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: appdb
      POSTGRES_USER: appuser
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"  # exposed to host for local DB tools
    volumes:
      - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
      - ./scripts/init.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init.sql
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U appuser -d appdb"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 20s
    networks:
      - app-network

  # ===== Redis =====
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    command: redis-server --requirepass ${REDIS_PASSWORD}
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"
    volumes:
      - redis-data:/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "-a", "${REDIS_PASSWORD}", "ping"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 3
    networks:
      - app-network

  # ===== Kafka (KRaft mode — no Zookeeper) =====
  kafka:
    image: confluentinc/cp-kafka:7.6.0
    ports:
      - "9092:9092"
    environment:
      KAFKA_NODE_ID: 1
      KAFKA_PROCESS_ROLES: broker,controller
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_QUORUM_VOTERS: 1@kafka:9093
      KAFKA_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://0.0.0.0:9092,CONTROLLER://0.0.0.0:9093
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://kafka:9092
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_LISTENER_NAMES: CONTROLLER
      KAFKA_LOG_DIRS: /var/lib/kafka/data
      CLUSTER_ID: MkU3OEVBNTcwNTJENDM2Qk
    volumes:
      - kafka-data:/var/lib/kafka/data
    networks:
      - app-network

volumes:
  postgres-data:
  redis-data:
  kafka-data:

networks:
  app-network:
    driver: bridge
```

## .env File

```bash
# .env — committed with safe defaults; override in CI/prod
DB_PASSWORD=devpassword
REDIS_PASSWORD=devredis
```

## Common Commands

```bash
docker compose up -d             # start all services in background
docker compose up -d app         # start only one service
docker compose logs -f app       # stream app logs
docker compose exec app /bin/sh  # shell into running container
docker compose down              # stop and remove containers
docker compose down -v           # also remove volumes (wipe data!)
docker compose ps                # show running services and health
docker compose restart app       # restart one service
```

speakable_v2.hook: Docker Compose lets you define an entire multi-container application in a single YAML file.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: The fix is to use depends_on with a health check condition, which waits until the dependency reports healthy before starting dependent services.

questions.title: Docker Compose Development Workflow
questions.question: How do you use Docker Compose effectively for local Java development with hot reload?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- docker-compose.override.yml: local overrides automatically merged — don't commit local-only config
- Profiles: --profile dev starts additional tools like pgAdmin, Redis Insight
- Volume mount for hot reload: mount compiled classes into container + Spring DevTools or JRebel
- Separate Compose files: base + dev + prod overlays (docker compose -f base.yml -f dev.yml)
- Health checks: ensure dependent services ready before app starts
- Testcontainers: alternative to Compose for integration tests — programmatic container management
- Docker Compose Watch: sync file changes directly into running containers (Compose v2.22+)

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The standard pattern for local development is running infrastructure services — PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka — in Docker while running the Spring Boot application directly on your machine with your IDE. This gives you fast restart cycles, full debugger support, and hot reload without the complexity of live-syncing files into a container.

For the cases where you do run the app in Docker, docker-compose.override.yml is automatically merged with the base file. You put development-specific overrides there — like mounting the target/classes directory and enabling Spring DevTools — and don't commit it. Each developer can have their own override without conflicting with the base configuration.

Testcontainers is worth mentioning here as an alternative for integration tests. Instead of starting Compose manually for tests, Testcontainers starts Docker containers programmatically at test startup and stops them when done. It gives you a clean, isolated database or Kafka for each test run, and everything is in code — no external Compose file to manage.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Recommended Dev Approach

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml — infrastructure only for local dev
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    ports: ["5432:5432"]
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: appdb
      POSTGRES_USER: appuser
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: devpassword
    volumes:
      - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U appuser"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 5

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    ports: ["6379:6379"]

  kafka:
    image: confluentinc/cp-kafka:7.6.0
    ports: ["9092:9092"]
    environment:
      KAFKA_NODE_ID: 1
      KAFKA_PROCESS_ROLES: broker,controller
      KAFKA_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://0.0.0.0:9092,CONTROLLER://0.0.0.0:9093
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://localhost:9092
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_QUORUM_VOTERS: 1@kafka:9093
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_LISTENER_NAMES: CONTROLLER
      CLUSTER_ID: MkU3OEVBNTcwNTJENDM2Qk

volumes:
  postgres-data:
```

```yaml
# docker-compose.override.yml — local dev tools (not committed)
services:
  pgadmin:
    image: dpage/pgadmin4
    ports: ["5050:80"]
    environment:
      PGADMIN_DEFAULT_EMAIL: dev@local.com
      PGADMIN_DEFAULT_PASSWORD: dev

  redis-insight:
    image: redis/redisinsight
    ports: ["5540:5540"]
```

```bash
# Start just infrastructure — run Spring Boot in IDE
docker compose up -d postgres redis kafka

# Then in IntelliJ/VS Code: run Spring Boot normally
# application-local.yml:
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/appdb  # localhost, not docker service name
  data:
    redis:
      host: localhost
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: localhost:9092
```

## Testcontainers for Integration Tests

```java
@SpringBootTest
@Testcontainers
class OrderServiceIntegrationTest {

    @Container
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine")
        .withDatabaseName("testdb")
        .withUsername("testuser")
        .withPassword("testpass");

    @Container
    static KafkaContainer kafka = new KafkaContainer(
        DockerImageName.parse("confluentinc/cp-kafka:7.6.0"));

    @DynamicPropertySource
    static void configureProperties(DynamicPropertyRegistry registry) {
        registry.add("spring.datasource.url", postgres::getJdbcUrl);
        registry.add("spring.datasource.username", postgres::getUsername);
        registry.add("spring.datasource.password", postgres::getPassword);
        registry.add("spring.kafka.bootstrap-servers", kafka::getBootstrapServers);
    }

    @Autowired OrderService orderService;

    @Test
    void should_create_order_and_publish_event() {
        Order order = orderService.createOrder(new CreateOrderRequest("user1", 99.99));
        assertThat(order.getId()).isNotNull();
        // Verify Kafka event was published...
    }
}
```

speakable_v2.cap: It gives you a clean, isolated database or Kafka for each test run, and everything is in code — no external Compose file to manage.

questions.title: Health Checks and Service Dependencies
questions.question: How do you properly handle startup order and health checks in Docker Compose?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- depends_on alone only controls start order — doesn't wait for readiness
- depends_on with condition: service_healthy waits for health check to pass
- Health check: test command + interval + timeout + retries + start_period
- start_period: grace period during startup — failures don't count toward retries
- Retry logic in app: Spring auto-reconnect for datasource, Kafka, Redis
- ENTRYPOINT scripts: wait-for-it.sh or dockerize to wait for TCP port
- Startup probes vs liveness vs readiness: Kubernetes patterns translate to Compose

sections.Title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The depends_on directive in Docker Compose only ensures services start in order — it doesn't wait for them to be actually ready. PostgreSQL might start accepting TCP connections before it's finished initializing its data directory. Your Spring Boot app might fail to connect in that window.

The proper solution is combining depends_on with a health check and a service_healthy condition. You define a health check command on the dependency — like pg_isready for PostgreSQL — and then your app service's depends_on specifies condition: service_healthy. Compose waits until the dependency's health check passes before starting the dependent service.

The start_period setting is important for services with slow startup. During the start period, failed health checks don't count toward the retry limit — this gives PostgreSQL time to initialize without being marked as unhealthy. After start_period, failures count and will eventually mark the container as unhealthy.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Health Checks per Service

```yaml
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: appdb
      POSTGRES_USER: appuser
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U appuser -d appdb"]
      interval: 10s       # check every 10s
      timeout: 5s         # fail if no response in 5s
      retries: 5          # fail after 5 consecutive failures
      start_period: 30s   # grace period — failures don't count during startup

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5

  kafka:
    image: confluentinc/cp-kafka:7.6.0
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "kafka-broker-api-versions --bootstrap-server localhost:9092"]
      interval: 15s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 60s  # Kafka takes longer to initialize

  app:
    build: .
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy  # waits for postgres healthcheck to pass
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
      kafka:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/actuator/health || exit 1"]
      interval: 30s
      start_period: 60s  # Spring Boot needs time to start
      retries: 3
```

## Application-Level Resilience

```yaml
# Even with health checks, add app-level retry for resilience
# application.yml
spring:
  datasource:
    hikari:
      initialization-fail-timeout: -1  # don't fail on startup if DB unavailable
  kafka:
    listener:
      missing-topics-fatal: false  # don't fail if topic doesn't exist yet
```

```java
// Resilience4j retry for external services
@Retry(name = "database", fallbackMethod = "fallbackMethod")
public Data fetchData() { ... }

// Or Spring Retry
@Retryable(
    value = {DataAccessException.class},
    maxAttempts = 5,
    backoff = @Backoff(delay = 2000, multiplier = 1.5)
)
public void startupTask() { ... }
```

speakable_v2.hook: The depends_on directive in Docker Compose only ensures services start in order — it doesn't wait for them to be actually ready.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: After start_period, failures count and will eventually mark the container as unhealthy.

questions.title: Environment Variables and Secrets in Docker Compose
questions.question: How do you manage environment variables and secrets securely in Docker Compose?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- environment: section — injects env vars; values visible in docker inspect
- .env file: auto-loaded by Compose — use for local default values, not committed secrets
- env_file: point to external .env file per service
- secrets: Docker Swarm native secrets — file-based; available at /run/secrets/
- For local dev: .env with safe dev values is fine; .gitignore it
- Production: use external secret manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) or Docker Swarm secrets
- Never hardcode passwords in docker-compose.yml — use variable substitution

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Docker Compose has several mechanisms for environment variables, each with different security trade-offs. The environment section in docker-compose.yml injects variables directly — convenient but the values are visible in the file itself, in docker inspect output, and in git history if committed.

The .env file is automatically loaded by Compose and its values are substituted into the compose file. The convention is to commit a .env.example with safe placeholder values and document what each variable is, then gitignore the actual .env with real credentials. This keeps secrets off of git while providing documentation of what needs to be configured.

For Docker Swarm-based production deployments, Docker Secrets are the proper solution — secrets are stored encrypted in Swarm and mounted as files at /run/secrets/ inside containers. Applications read the file instead of an environment variable, which prevents secrets from appearing in process listings or docker inspect output.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Variable Substitution Patterns

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  app:
    environment:
      # Direct value — visible in file and docker inspect
      SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: dev

      # Variable substitution from .env file
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}

      # With default value if not set
      SERVER_PORT: ${SERVER_PORT:-8080}

      # Mandatory — Compose fails if not set
      JWT_SECRET: ${JWT_SECRET:?JWT_SECRET must be set in .env}
```

```bash
# .env.example (COMMIT THIS — shows what's needed)
DB_PASSWORD=change_me
REDIS_PASSWORD=change_me
JWT_SECRET=change_me_to_long_random_string
SMTP_PASSWORD=change_me

# .env (GITIGNORED — real local values)
DB_PASSWORD=mydevpassword
REDIS_PASSWORD=mydevredis
JWT_SECRET=development-jwt-secret-32-chars-long
SMTP_PASSWORD=realsmtppass
```

```bash
# .gitignore
.env
!.env.example
*.env.local
```

## Docker Swarm Secrets (Production)

```bash
# Create secret in Swarm
echo 'my-super-secret-db-password' | docker secret create db_password -

# Or from file
docker secret create ssl_cert ./path/to/cert.pem
```

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml for Swarm
services:
  app:
    secrets:
      - db_password
      - ssl_cert
    environment:
      # Application reads from /run/secrets/db_password
      DB_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/db_password

secrets:
  db_password:
    external: true  # created with docker secret create
  ssl_cert:
    external: true
```

```java
// Application reads secret from file (Spring Boot)
// application.yml:
// spring.datasource.password: ${DB_PASSWORD:${DB_PASSWORD_FILE:}}

@Value("${DB_PASSWORD_FILE:}")
String passwordFile;

@PostConstruct
void loadSecret() throws IOException {
    if (!passwordFile.isBlank()) {
        String password = Files.readString(Path.of(passwordFile)).trim();
        // Use password...
    }
}
```

speakable_v2.hook: Docker Compose has several mechanisms for environment variables, each with different security trade-offs.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Applications read the file instead of an environment variable, which prevents secrets from appearing in process listings or docker inspect output.

questions.title: Docker Networking Deep Dive
questions.question: How does Docker networking work and what are the different network drivers?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- bridge: default — virtual network, containers communicate by name; host ports mapped explicitly
- host: container shares host's network stack — best performance, no isolation
- overlay: multi-host networking — Docker Swarm; containers on different hosts communicate
- macvlan: container gets its own MAC/IP on host network — appears as physical device
- none: no networking — complete isolation
- Compose default network: custom bridge — containers reach each other by service name
- DNS: Docker provides built-in DNS — service names resolve within the same network
- Port mapping: hostPort:containerPort — 8080:8080 maps host port to container port

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Docker containers communicate through networks. The bridge network is the default — Docker creates a virtual network interface, assigns IP addresses to containers, and provides DNS resolution by container/service name. Containers on the same bridge network can reach each other by name without any additional configuration.

Docker Compose creates a dedicated bridge network for each project automatically. All services in a Compose file join this network, which is why your spring-boot app can connect to postgres:5432 by using the service name 'postgres' as the hostname. The names come from the service definitions in docker-compose.yml.

Host networking is available when you need maximum performance and don't need container network isolation — the container uses the host's network stack directly, eliminating the virtual network overhead. This is occasionally used for network-intensive applications but sacrifices the isolation benefit of containers.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Compose Network Connectivity

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"  # Host 8080 → Container 8080
    environment:
      # Use service names as hostnames — Docker DNS resolves them
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/appdb
      SPRING_DATA_REDIS_HOST: redis
      SPRING_KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS: kafka:9092
    networks:
      - backend

  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    # NOT exposed to host — only accessible within backend network
    networks:
      - backend

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    networks:
      - backend

  # Admin tool — separate frontend network
  pgadmin:
    image: dpage/pgadmin4
    ports:
      - "5050:80"
    networks:
      - backend   # can reach postgres
      - frontend  # exposed to host

networks:
  backend:    # internal — no external access
    driver: bridge
  frontend:   # external access
    driver: bridge
```

## Network Inspection

```bash
# List networks
docker network ls

# Inspect: see which containers are on the network, their IPs
docker network inspect myproject_backend

# Connect a running container to a network
docker network connect backend my-container

# Check DNS resolution inside container
docker exec -it my-app-container nslookup postgres
# Address 1: 172.18.0.3 postgres.myproject_backend
```

## Port Mapping Options

```yaml
ports:
  - "8080:8080"       # host:container — map host port to container port
  - "8080"            # random host port → container 8080
  - "127.0.0.1:8080:8080"  # bind to localhost only — not exposed externally
  - "8080-8090:8080-8090"  # range mapping
```

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: This is occasionally used for network-intensive applications but sacrifices the isolation benefit of containers.

questions.title: Docker Best Practices for Java Production
questions.question: What are the production best practices for running Java applications in Docker?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Non-root user: always run as non-root in production — security
- Read-only filesystem: --read-only flag with tmpfs mounts for temp files
- Health checks: HEALTHCHECK directive or health check in orchestrator
- Graceful shutdown: handle SIGTERM — Spring Boot does this by default
- Logging: stdout/stderr only — let orchestrator handle log routing
- Image scanning: trivy, snyk, or AWS ECR scanning for CVEs
- Pinned base images: use specific tags (eclipse-temurin:21.0.3_9-jre-alpine), not just '21'
- Signal forwarding: use exec form ENTRYPOINT, not shell form — ensures PID 1 gets signals

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Running containers as root is a significant security risk. If an attacker escapes the container, they have root privileges on the host. Always create a non-root user in your Dockerfile and switch to it before the ENTRYPOINT. This is a requirement in many security-conscious environments and a best practice everywhere.

The ENTRYPOINT form matters for signal handling. Shell form — ENTRYPOINT java -jar app.jar — runs your app as a child of /bin/sh, which is PID 1. When Docker sends SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, it goes to /bin/sh, not to Java. Exec form — ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"] — makes Java PID 1 and receives signals directly. Spring Boot needs SIGTERM to trigger its graceful shutdown, closing connections and finishing in-flight requests.

Health checks are essential for orchestrators. A container that has started isn't necessarily healthy — Spring Boot might still be initializing, running migrations, or waiting for external dependencies. The HEALTHCHECK directive or Kubernetes/ECS health check configuration tells the orchestrator when the container is actually ready to accept traffic.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Production-Ready Dockerfile

```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine AS runtime
WORKDIR /app

# Non-root user
RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup

# Copy app as root, then switch user
COPY --chown=appuser:appgroup target/app.jar app.jar

USER appuser

# Graceful shutdown: Spring Boot waits for in-flight requests
# Needs: server.shutdown=graceful in application.yml
ENV JAVA_OPTS="\
  -XX:+UseContainerSupport \
  -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 \
  -XX:+UseG1GC \
  -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8"

EXPOSE 8080

# HEALTHCHECK: orchestrators use this to know when app is ready
HEALTHCHECK \
  --interval=30s \
  --timeout=5s \
  --start-period=60s \
  --retries=3 \
  CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/actuator/health | grep -q '"status":"UP"' || exit 1

# Exec form: Java is PID 1, receives SIGTERM for graceful shutdown
ENTRYPOINT ["sh", "-c", "exec java $JAVA_OPTS -jar app.jar"]
# 'exec' replaces sh with java → java becomes PID 1
```

## Graceful Shutdown Configuration

```yaml
# application.yml
server:
  shutdown: graceful  # wait for in-flight requests to complete
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 30s  # max wait time
```

## Image Scanning in CI

```bash
# Trivy: scan Docker image for CVEs
trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL my-app:latest
# --exit-code 1: fail CI if CRITICAL CVEs found

# In GitHub Actions:
- name: Scan image for vulnerabilities
  uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
  with:
    image-ref: '${{ steps.build.outputs.image }}'
    format: 'sarif'
    exit-code: '1'
    severity: 'CRITICAL,HIGH'
```

## Logging Best Practice

```java
// Always log to stdout — NOT to files
// application.yml
logging:
  file:
    name: ""  # don't log to file in container
  pattern:
    console: "%d{ISO8601} %-5level [%X{traceId}] %logger{36} - %msg%n"
// Docker / Kubernetes routes stdout to log aggregator (EFK, Loki, CloudWatch)
```

speakable_v2.hook: Running containers as root is a significant security risk.
speakable_v2.cap: The HEALTHCHECK directive or Kubernetes/ECS health check configuration tells the orchestrator when the container is actually ready to accept traffic.
